# ReadingTracks

> Papers, researchers, venues, and reading tracks for a Systems & AI reading club. A hand-curated catalog of 313 papers grouped into 45 reading tracks, with 326 'read A before B' edges.

The catalog's value is its curation: which papers belong together and what to read first. Edges are conceptual reading-order hints, not a citation graph. Prefer the structured data below over scraping the HTML page.

## Data

- [Graph JSON](https://eribeiro.github.io/reading-tracks/data/edges.json): papers (nodes), reading-order edges, and tracks in one file
- [Papers YAML](https://eribeiro.github.io/reading-tracks/data/papers.yaml): source of truth for papers and tracks
- [Researchers YAML](https://eribeiro.github.io/reading-tracks/data/researchers.yaml): researchers and their papers
- [Venues YAML](https://eribeiro.github.io/reading-tracks/data/venues.yaml): curated venue list
- [Site](https://eribeiro.github.io/reading-tracks/): interactive browser with filters and the Tracks view

## Tracks

### AI Database Systems

- [The Case for Learned Index Structures (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3183713.3196909): What if database indexes were learned models? Opened the agenda of applying ML to database components.
- [Bao: Making Learned Query Optimization Practical (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3448016.3452838): Wraps a conventional optimizer with a learned plan-selection policy, retaining dependable search while adapting choices to observed execution performance.
- [Milvus: A Purpose-Built Vector Data Management System (2021)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3448016.3457550): A data management system purpose-built for large-scale approximate nearest-neighbor search over vectors — the data-infrastructure piece underneath embeddings, semantic search, and RAG in the modern AI stack.
- [DILI: A Distribution-Driven Learned Index (2023)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol16/p2212-li.pdf): Builds an update-capable learned tree whose fanout and leaf models follow local key distributions, balancing model accuracy against traversal depth.
- [Algorithmic Complexity Attacks on Dynamic Learned Indexes (2023)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p780-yang.pdf): Shows how carefully chosen inserts can drive a dynamic learned index into extreme memory use or thousand-fold slowdowns, making worst-case robustness part of index design.
- [Learned Index: A Comprehensive Experimental Evaluation (2023)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol16/p1992-li.pdf): Tests learned and traditional indexes under one framework, exposing where model-based designs help and where updates, strings, concurrency, and range scans erase their advantage.
- [Making In-Memory Learned Indexes Efficient on Disk (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3654954): Derives six storage-aware transformations that turn memory-first learned indexes into disk layouts that improve both throughput and space over B+ trees.
- [Accelerating String-key Learned Index Structures via Memoization-based Incremental Training (2024)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p1802-park.pdf): Reuses prior model-training work for updated string keys and offloads retraining to an FPGA, attacking the cost that makes mutable string learned indexes impractical.
- [DobLIX: A Dual-Objective Learned Index for Log-Structured Merge Trees (2025)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p3965-heidari.pdf): Co-optimizes learned-model accuracy and physical block access inside RocksDB, adapting its LSM index and data layout as workloads change.
- [Optimizing LLM Queries in Relational Data Analytics Workloads (2025)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2025): A direct bridge between traditional query optimization and analytical workloads that incorporate LLM calls.
- [Text2SQL is Not Enough: Unifying AI and Databases with TAG (2025)](https://vldb.org/cidrdb/2025/text2sql-is-not-enough-unifying-ai-and-Databases-with-tag.html): Proposes a broader abstraction than Text-to-SQL for combining model reasoning with scalable data processing.
- [Why Are Learned Indexes So Effective but Sometimes Ineffective? (2025)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p2886-liu.pdf): Reconciles the PGM-index's strong asymptotic bounds with memory-bound execution in practice, then uses that diagnosis to build the faster PGM++.

### AI Runtime Scheduling

- [Gandiva: Introspective Cluster Scheduling for Deep Learning (2018)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi18/presentation/xiao): Introspects into DL training jobs — mini-batch boundaries, memory footprint — to enable fine-grained time-slicing and packing of jobs onto GPUs, something opaque batch schedulers like Borg/Omega can't do.
- [Ray: A Distributed Framework for Emerging AI Applications (2018)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi18/presentation/moritz): A distributed execution engine built around a unified task-and-actor API and a decentralized, bottom-up scheduler, designed for the fine-grained, dynamic task graphs typical of reinforcement learning rather than static DAGs.
- [Salus: Fine-Grained GPU Sharing Primitives for Deep Learning Applications (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04610): Introduces fast iteration-level GPU sharing and memory-lane primitives that let training jobs coexist without the overhead of process-level time slicing.
- [Rubick: Exploiting Job Reconfigurability for Deep Learning Cluster Scheduling (2025)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2025): Continues the Borg/Omega/Gandiva/Pollux lineage, bringing scheduling to dynamically reconfigurable deep-learning jobs.
- [SOLA: Optimizing SLO Attainment for Large Language Model Serving with State-Aware Scheduling (2025)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2025): Represents the post-vLLM generation of schedulers that treat state and SLOs as central elements of serving.
- [ThunderServe: High-performance and Cost-efficient LLM Serving in Cloud Environments (2025)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/c2a0e26dd9ee7d57e92bb1c24b39659a-Abstract-Conference.html): Explores LLM serving across heterogeneous clouds and makes cost, network, and placement an explicit part of the optimization.
- [Efficient LLM Serving on Commodity GPU Clusters with Data-Reduced Cross-Instance Orchestration (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/technical-sessions): Shows how to adapt prefill/decode disaggregation to clusters without cutting-edge interconnects, a relevant constraint outside hyperscalers.
- [Prism: Cost-Efficient Multi-LLM Serving via GPU Memory Ballooning (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/technical-sessions): Turns multi-model serving into an explicit problem of dynamic memory management and GPU efficiency.
- [PROMPTS: PeRformance Optimization via Multi-Agent Planning for LLM Training and Serving (2026)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2026/hash/48253da5351effdfea994fd7bbff7005-Abstract-Conference.html): A recent example of AI being used to optimize its own training and serving infrastructure.
- [SuperInfer: SLO-Aware Rotary Scheduling and Memory Management for LLM Inference on Superchips (2026)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2026): Represents the recent specialization of inference schedulers for new accelerator and memory topologies.

### Analytical Databases

- [C-Store: A Column-oriented DBMS (2005)](https://www.vldb.org/archives/website/2005/program/paper/thu/p553-stonebraker.pdf): A column-oriented DBMS built from scratch for read-heavy analytics, with column-specific compression, multiple overlapping sort orders, and a write-optimized store merged in the background — the direct research ancestor of Vertica.
- [Dremel: Interactive Analysis of Web-Scale Datasets (2010)](https://doi.org/10.14778/1920841.1920886): Interactive queries over trillions of rows; the nested-data columnar storage that became the basis for BigQuery.
- [MonetDB: Two Decades of Research in Column-oriented Database Architectures (2012)](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/19929): A compact architectural history of MonetDB that connects columnar storage, CPU-conscious execution, adaptive indexing, run-time optimization, and modular system design across two decades of CWI research.
- [The SAP HANA Database -- An Architecture Overview (2012)](http://sites.computer.org/debull/A12mar/hana.pdf): An architectural view of HANA's hybrid row/column engine, with a focus on hardware-conscious design for compression and columnar processing — the most-cited architectural reference for HANA in the systems literature.
- [The Vertica Analytic Database: C-Store 7 Years Later (2012)](https://vldb.org/pvldb/vol5/p1790_andrewlamb_vldb2012.pdf): A rare "research became product" retrospective — written largely by original C-Store authors — on which academic ideas survived contact with real customers and workloads when C-Store became Vertica, and which didn't.
- [DB2 with BLU Acceleration: So Much More than Just a Column Store (2013)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol6/p1080-barber.pdf): How a mature row-store RDBMS (DB2) gained an in-memory columnar engine without requiring separate tuning — order-preserving frequency compression lets predicates, joins, and group-bys run directly on compressed, bit-packed values via SIMD.
- [Distributed Architecture of Oracle Database In-memory (2015)](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p1630-mukherjee.pdf): Oracle Database In-Memory's dual-format architecture — a row store for OLTP and an in-memory column store for analytics, kept transactionally consistent — and how it scales across a distributed RAC cluster.
- [DuckDB: An Embeddable Analytical Database (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3299869.3320212): Embedded columnar OLAP in a single process; the vectorized execution of X100/MonetDB taken to its practical extreme.
- [Presto: SQL on Everything (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDE.2019.00196): Presents a production distributed SQL engine that queries heterogeneous data sources in place rather than requiring them to be loaded into one warehouse.
- [Napa: Powering Scalable Data Warehousing with Robust Query Performance at Google (2021)](https://research.google/pubs/napa-powering-scalable-data-warehousing-with-robust-query-performance-at-google/): A production account of Google's Napa warehouse, which combines continuous geo-distributed ingestion, strongly consistent materialized views, sub-second queries, and explicit tradeoffs among freshness, performance, and cost.
- [Photon: A Fast Query Engine for Lakehouse Systems (2022)](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~matei/papers/2022/sigmod_photon.pdf): Databricks' vectorized C++ query engine for querying lakehouse data directly on cloud object storage via both SQL and Spark's DataFrame API — set a new 100TB TPC-DS record. Won Best Industrial Paper at SIGMOD 2022.
- [Progressive Partitioning for Parallelized Query Execution in Google's Napa (2023)](https://research.google/pubs/progressive-partitioning-for-parallelized-query-execution-in-googles-napa/): Explains how Napa progressively partitions an LSM forest within a strict planning budget, producing sufficiently balanced per-query work assignments despite skew and enabling billions of low-latency reporting queries each day.
- [ClickHouse - Lightning Fast Analytics for Everyone (2024)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p3731-schulze.pdf): ClickHouse's first formal research paper, covering the MergeTree storage family, SIMD-vectorized execution, and adaptive query execution — a widely deployed open-source column store developed independently of the C-Store lineage.

### Batch To Dataflow

- [MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters (2004)](https://research.google/pubs/mapreduce-simplified-data-processing-on-large-clusters/): A two-function programming model (map/reduce) plus a runtime that handles partitioning, scheduling, and failure recovery automatically — the paper that made batch processing over thousands of commodity machines routine.
- [Dryad: Distributed Data-Parallel Programs from Sequential Building Blocks (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1272996.1273005): Generalizes MapReduce jobs into arbitrary dataflow graphs built from sequential programs, anticipating the execution model of later analytics engines.
- [MapReduce and Parallel DBMSs: Friends or Foes? (2010)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1629175.1629197): Compares parallel-DBMS engineering with the MapReduce/Hadoop paradigm and concludes they're complementary — a central artifact of the 'specialized architecture vs. one size fits all' debate.
- [Large-scale Incremental Processing Using Distributed Transactions and Notifications (2010)](https://research.google/pubs/large-scale-incremental-processing-using-distributed-transactions-and-notifications/): Percolator fills the gap between batch MapReduce and online databases by combining small ACID transactions with notifications, enabling Google to update its web index incrementally at enormous scale.
- [CIEL: A Universal Execution Engine for Distributed Data-Flow Computing (2011)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi11/ciel-universal-execution-engine-distributed-data-flow-computing): Generalizes earlier batch dataflow engines (MapReduce/Dryad) by letting tasks make data-dependent control-flow decisions at runtime, enabling iterative and recursive computations with transparent fault tolerance.
- [Resilient Distributed Datasets: A Fault-Tolerant Abstraction for In-Memory Cluster Computing (2012)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi12/technical-sessions/presentation/zaharia): Introduces Resilient Distributed Datasets — read-only, lineage-tracked collections that recompute lost partitions instead of replicating data — enabling in-memory reuse across iterative jobs that MapReduce forced back to disk every step.
- [The Dataflow Model: A Practical Approach to Balancing Correctness, Latency, and Cost in Massive-Scale, Unbounded, Out-of-Order Data Processing (2015)](https://doi.org/10.14778/2824032.2824076): Unified batch and streaming into a single model of windows and event time; the conceptual basis for Beam and Flink.

### Causality Tracking

- [Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System (1978)](https://doi.org/10.1145/359545.359563): Shows that in a distributed system with no shared clock, you can still define a consistent 'happens-before' partial order using logical clocks — the foundation nearly every later consistency and consensus protocol builds on.
- [Detection of Mutual Inconsistency in Distributed Systems (1983)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.1983.236733): Introduces version vectors to detect when replicated copies of a file diverged during a network partition, the mechanism later inherited by Dynamo-style stores.
- [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (2007)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1323293.1294281): The seminal paper on Dynamo's architecture — consistent hashing, sloppy quorums, vector clocks, gossip, and availability as an explicit design priority.
- [Eventually Consistent (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1435417.1435432): A practitioner's tour of the consistency spectrum between strong and eventual, and of the client-side guarantees that make weak consistency usable at Amazon scale.
- [Dotted Version Vectors: Logical Clocks for Optimistic Replication (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.5808): Shows why server-id and client-id version vectors either lose causality or grow without bound, and introduces dotted version vectors as an exact clock sized by the replication degree.
- [Brief Announcement: Efficient Causality Tracking in Distributed Storage Systems with Dotted Version Vectors (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2332432.2332497): A two-page statement of the dotted version vector idea, separating a version's identifier from its causal past so that causality checks take constant time.
- [Scalable and Accurate Causality Tracking for Eventually Consistent Stores (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-43352-2_6): Gives the full treatment of dotted version vectors and introduces DVV sets, a compact per-key clock for all siblings, together with a small kernel of operations any key-value store clock must implement.
- [Logical Physical Clocks (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-14472-6_2): Combines causal ordering with timestamps close to physical time, making logical-clock guarantees practical for snapshots and transactions in distributed databases.
- [Why Logical Clocks Are Easy (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2890782): Derives causal histories, vector clocks, version vectors, and dotted version vectors from one idea, tracking the set of events that precede each event, so the update rules follow from it.

### Cloud Databases

- [Amazon Redshift and the Case for Simpler Data Warehouses (2015)](https://www.amazon.science/publications/amazon-redshift-and-the-case-for-simpler-data-warehouses): The original Redshift paper explains how managed provisioning, automatic maintenance, workload-aware tuning, and a scale-out columnar engine made data warehousing accessible beyond specialist enterprise teams.
- [The Snowflake Elastic Data Warehouse (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2882903.2903741): Separates storage, compute, and cloud services into independently scalable layers running entirely on commodity cloud infrastructure, letting warehouses scale up, down, or out without moving data.
- [Amazon Aurora: Design Considerations for High Throughput Cloud-Native Relational Databases (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3035918.3056101): Pushes redo logging down into a distributed, multi-tenant storage service and ships only log records, not pages, over the network, cutting I/O on the write path to make replication nearly free.
- [Amazon Aurora: On Avoiding Distributed Consensus for I/Os, Commits, and Membership Changes (2018)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3183713.3196937): The companion paper to the 2017 Aurora paper, explaining how Aurora avoids expensive distributed-consensus protocols on the hot paths of I/O, commit, and storage-quorum membership changes, pushing consensus only to rare membership events. A concrete engineering pattern that shaped how other cloud-native databases reason about latency versus durability.
- [F1 Query: Declarative Querying at Scale (2018)](https://research.google/pubs/f1-query-declarative-querying-at-scale/): The key F1 follow-on for query processing, describing a production federated SQL platform that spans files and storage systems while supporting point queries, interactive analytics, and large ETL pipelines.
- [Adapting to Access Locality via Live Data Migration in Globally Distributed Datastores (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1109/BigData.2018.8622565): Defines practical requirements for moving live data toward changing demand while preserving availability, load balance, and low access latency.
- [PolarFS: An Ultra-low Latency and Failure Resilient Distributed File System for Shared Storage Cloud Database (2018)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol11/p1849-cao.pdf): The ultra-low-latency distributed file system (RDMA, NVMe, user-space I/O stack) underlying PolarDB's shared-storage architecture — the concrete storage layer behind what's often called "the Chinese Aurora."
- [AnalyticDB: Real-time OLAP Database System at Alibaba Cloud (2019)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol12/p2059-zhan.pdf): Alibaba Cloud's distributed OLAP system for low-latency ad-hoc analytical queries over rapidly-changing data, maintaining asynchronous all-column indexes to keep freshness and interactivity together.
- [Socrates: The New SQL Server in the Cloud (2019)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/socrates.pdf): Microsoft's cloud-native re-architecture of SQL Server (underlying Azure SQL Database Hyperscale), treating the transaction log itself as a separately-scaled distributed service decoupled from page storage. A direct architectural sibling to Aurora, but pushing the log/page split even further.
- [CockroachDB: The Resilient Geo-Distributed SQL Database (2020)](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/pdf/cockroachdb-the-resilient-geo-distributed-sql-database-sigmod-2020.pdf): Extends the Spanner lineage directly — Raft-replicated, horizontally-scalable SQL with serializable geo-distributed transactions — but without Spanner's specialized TrueTime hardware, using hybrid-logical clocks instead.
- [F1 Lightning: HTAP as a Service (2020)](https://research.google/pubs/f1-lightning-htap-as-a-service/): A production HTAP case study for brownfield environments, showing how Google added fast analytical access across existing transactional systems without requiring the query service to own or replace them.
- [TiDB: A Raft-based HTAP Database (2020)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p3072-huang.pdf): Pairs a Raft-replicated row store with an asynchronously-replicated columnar store (via Raft learners) to serve HTAP workloads on the same transactionally-consistent data — explicitly positioned as following the NewSQL lineage of CockroachDB and Spanner.
- [Napa: Powering Scalable Data Warehousing with Robust Query Performance at Google (2021)](https://research.google/pubs/napa-powering-scalable-data-warehousing-with-robust-query-performance-at-google/): A production account of Google's Napa warehouse, which combines continuous geo-distributed ingestion, strongly consistent materialized views, sub-second queries, and explicit tradeoffs among freshness, performance, and cost.
- [Amazon DynamoDB: A Scalable, Predictably Performant, and Fully Managed NoSQL Database Service (2022)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc22/presentation/elhemali): Shows how Dynamo's ideas evolved into a fully managed, multi-tenant service with strict scale and predictability goals.
- [OceanBase: A 707 Million tpmC Distributed Relational Database System (2022)](https://vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p3385-xu.pdf): The engineering behind OceanBase's record 707-million-tpmC TPC-C result — a Paxos-based, shared-nothing distributed relational database with cross-region fault tolerance and multi-tenancy, now maintained primarily by Ant Group. A landmark industry paper on scaling distributed OLTP.
- [Amazon Redshift Re-invented (2022)](https://assets.amazon.science/93/e0/a347021a4c6fbbccd5a056580d00/sigmod22-redshift-reinvented.pdf): An industrial case study of migrating a decade-old shared-nothing MPP warehouse to a cloud-native architecture with independently scalable compute and storage, materialized-view-based caching, and self-tuning autonomics — while keeping tens of thousands of existing customers running.
- [Cloud-Native Transactions and Analytics in SingleStore (2022)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3514221.3526055): TiDB's HTAP counterpart from a different vendor — distributed SQL re-architected for disaggregated cloud compute and storage, running OLTP and OLAP over the same data.
- [Distributed Transactions at Scale in Amazon DynamoDB (2023)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc23/presentation/idziorek): Complements the DynamoDB paper by explaining how the service offers distributed ACID transactions without giving up its scale and availability requirements.
- [Progressive Partitioning for Parallelized Query Execution in Google's Napa (2023)](https://research.google/pubs/progressive-partitioning-for-parallelized-query-execution-in-googles-napa/): Explains how Napa progressively partitions an LSM forest within a strict planning budget, producing sufficiently balanced per-query work assignments despite skew and enabling billions of low-latency reporting queries each day.
- [Aurora DSQL: Scalable, Multi-Region OLTP (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13276): An end-to-end description of Aurora DSQL — a disaggregated architecture with MVCC and precision timestamps for coordination-free reads and OCC for writes, deferring coordination to commit time. A direct evolution of the original Aurora toward active-active multi-region.
- [WriteGuards: Distributed Storage Support for Strongly Consistent Caches (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/technical-sessions): Reopens a classic problem — strongly consistent caching — with a lightweight storage primitive, evaluated on TiDB.

### Cluster Scheduling

- [Dominant Resource Fairness: Fair Allocation of Multiple Resource Types (2011)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi11/dominant-resource-fairness-fair-allocation-multiple-resource-types): Extends max-min fairness to heterogeneous resources and provides the allocation principle behind influential multi-tenant cluster schedulers.
- [Mesos: A Platform for Fine-Grained Resource Sharing in the Data Center (2011)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi11/mesos-platform-fine-grained-resource-sharing-data-center): Splits cluster scheduling into a thin resource-offer layer plus pluggable per-framework schedulers, letting Hadoop, Spark, and others share a cluster without one scheduler needing to understand every workload.
- [Omega: Flexible, Scalable Schedulers for Large Compute Clusters (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2465351.2465386): Replaces a single centralized scheduler with optimistic concurrency over a shared cluster-state store, letting multiple schedulers propose placements in parallel and resolve conflicts at commit time.
- [Large-scale Cluster Management at Google with Borg (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2741948.2741964): Google's cluster manager packing heterogeneous batch and long-running jobs onto shared machines at high utilization via priorities and preemption — the internal system Kubernetes was built to bring to everyone else.
- [Musketeer: All for One, One for All in Data Processing Systems (2015)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2741948.2741968): Decouples how big-data workflows are expressed from which engine executes them, compiling a single specification down to Hadoop, Spark, Naiad, or PowerGraph as best fits — an execution-layer answer to the heterogeneity that Omega/Firmament tackle at the scheduling layer.
- [Borg, Omega, and Kubernetes: Lessons Learned from Three Container-Management Systems over a Decade (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2890784): A short, readable retrospective on what Google learned moving from one scheduler to the next, up through Kubernetes.
- [Firmament: Fast, Centralized Cluster Scheduling at Scale (2016)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi16/technical-sessions/presentation/gog): Centralized scheduling modeled as min-cost flow, fast enough for large clusters.
- [TetriSched: Global Rescheduling with Adaptive Plan-ahead in Dynamic Heterogeneous Clusters (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2901318.2901355): Continuously re-evaluates the scheduling plan every cycle using job deadlines and duration estimates to decide between waiting for a preferred resource or falling back to an alternative. Won Best Student Paper at EuroSys 2016.
- [Learning Scheduling Algorithms for Data Processing Clusters (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.01963): Uses graph neural networks and reinforcement learning to learn scheduling policies for DAG-structured data-processing jobs, beating carefully tuned heuristics — a central reference for the 'learned systems' theme.
- [Pollux: Co-adaptive Cluster Scheduling for Goodput-Optimized Deep Learning (2021)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi21/presentation/qiao): Schedules DL training by optimizing 'goodput,' jointly adjusting resources and batch size. A direct heir to Gandiva.
- [Rubick: Exploiting Job Reconfigurability for Deep Learning Cluster Scheduling (2025)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2025): Continues the Borg/Omega/Gandiva/Pollux lineage, bringing scheduling to dynamically reconfigurable deep-learning jobs.

### Consensus Replication

- [Viewstamped Replication: A New Primary Copy Method to Support Highly-Available Distributed Systems (1988)](https://doi.org/10.1145/62546.62549): One of the earliest primary-backup replication protocols with automatic view changes on primary failure — predates Paxos-based replicated state machines but solves essentially the same problem.
- [The Part-Time Parliament (1998)](https://doi.org/10.1145/279227.279229): Introduces Paxos via a parliamentary allegory — a group of processes agreeing on a single value despite lost messages and participants coming and going, using overlapping majority quorums.
- [Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (1999)](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/osdi99/full_papers/castro/castro.pdf): The first BFT protocol practical enough for real systems; the basis for much of the later work on Byzantine fault tolerance.
- [Chain Replication for Supporting High Throughput and Availability (2004)](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/osdi04/tech/full_papers/renesse/renesse.pdf): Replicates by chaining nodes so writes flow head-to-tail and reads hit the tail, giving strong consistency with throughput that scales independently of failure tolerance, unlike quorum-based schemes.
- [The Chubby Lock Service for Loosely-Coupled Distributed Systems (2006)](https://static.usenix.org/events/osdi06/tech/burrows.html): Shows why it's useful to encapsulate consensus in a high-level coordination service used by other systems like GFS and Bigtable.
- [Paxos Made Live: An Engineering Perspective (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1281100.1281103): A frank account of everything the original Paxos paper leaves out — disk corruption, group membership changes, making the algorithm fast enough for production — showing consensus theory and consensus engineering aren't the same thing.
- [There Is More Consensus in Egalitarian Parliaments (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2517349.2517350): Removes the stable-leader bottleneck for non-conflicting commands and achieves a one-WAN-round-trip fast path from any replica.
- [In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft) (2014)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc14/technical-sessions/presentation/ongaro): Redesigns consensus explicitly for understandability — strong leader election, log matching, and membership changes as separate, teachable sub-problems — without sacrificing Paxos's safety guarantees.
- [Raft Refloated: Do We Have Consensus? (2015)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2723872.2723876): An independent, critical reimplementation of Raft shortly after the original paper, simulation-testing its 'understandability' claims and pointing out optimizations.
- [Flexible Paxos: Quorum Intersection Revisited (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.06696): Shows that Paxos quorums only need to intersect across different phases, not within the same phase — a generalization that opens the door to asymmetric, more available quorums.
- [Dissecting the Performance of Strongly-Consistent Replication Protocols (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3299869.3319893): Systematically compares single-leader, multi-leader, hierarchical, and leaderless consensus protocols across LAN and WAN conditions, connecting protocol design choices to practical latency and throughput.
- [Distributed Consensus Revised (2019)](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-935.pdf): A PhD thesis that synthesizes and generalizes Flexible Paxos, re-deriving Paxos's correctness from weaker premises — the definitive reference for Heidi Howard's work on consensus.
- [Linearizable Quorum Reads in Paxos (2019)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/hotstorage19/presentation/charapko): Provides linearizable reads through follower quorums without depending on a stable leader or bounded-clock leases, offering a useful contrast with LeaseGuard.
- [Paxos vs Raft: Have We Reached Consensus on Distributed Consensus? (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05074): Rewrites Paxos using Raft's terminology to compare the two protocols side by side — concludes they're more alike than either one's reputation suggests.
- [WPaxos: Wide Area Network Flexible Consensus (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TPDS.2019.2929793): Combines flexible quorums, multiple leaders, and dynamic object ownership to make strongly consistent replication responsive to shifting access locality across geographic regions.
- [PigPaxos: Devouring the Communication Bottlenecks in Distributed Consensus (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3448016.3452834): Relieves the Paxos leader's communication bottleneck with rotating relay nodes and acknowledgment aggregation while preserving strong consistency.
- [BunchBFT: Across-Cluster Consensus Protocol (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10658): Explores a hierarchical, cluster-based BFT design that reduces wide-area communication costs while retaining consensus safety and liveness.
- [How to Evaluate Distributed Coordination Systems? A Survey and Analysis (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TPDS.2025.3631614): Provides a current framework for evaluating coordination systems across performance, scalability, availability, consistency, and fault tolerance instead of relying on incomparable ad hoc benchmarks.
- [LeaseGuard: Raft Leases Done Right (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.15659): Turns Raft's log into a rigorously specified leader lease, enabling zero-round-trip consistent reads while preserving high read and write availability during leader failover.

### Coordination Services

- [The Chubby Lock Service for Loosely-Coupled Distributed Systems (2006)](https://static.usenix.org/events/osdi06/tech/burrows.html): Shows why it's useful to encapsulate consensus in a high-level coordination service used by other systems like GFS and Bigtable.
- [ZooKeeper: Wait-free Coordination for Internet-scale Systems (2010)](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/atc10/tech/full_papers/Hunt.pdf): A wait-free coordination service exposing a small filesystem-like API (znodes, watches) with sequential consistency, letting applications build locks, leader election, and configuration management without embedding their own consensus.
- [Efficient Distributed Coordination at WAN-Scale (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDCS.2017.274): Extends ZooKeeper-style coordination across regions with a hierarchy and migrating autonomy tokens that exploit access locality.
- [How to Evaluate Distributed Coordination Systems? A Survey and Analysis (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TPDS.2025.3631614): Provides a current framework for evaluating coordination systems across performance, scalability, availability, consistency, and fault tolerance instead of relying on incomparable ad hoc benchmarks.
- [WriteGuards: Distributed Storage Support for Strongly Consistent Caches (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/technical-sessions): Reopens a classic problem — strongly consistent caching — with a lightweight storage primitive, evaluated on TiDB.

### Database Architecture

- [Query Evaluation Techniques for Large Databases (1993)](https://doi.org/10.1145/152610.152611): Graefe's landmark survey unifies the implementation principles behind iterators, sorting, hashing, set-matching, complex plans, extensibility, and parallel query execution into a durable foundation for engine design.
- [The Five-Minute Rule Ten Years Later, and Other Computer Storage Rules of Thumb (1997)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/the-five-minute-rule-ten-years-later/): Translates hardware price and performance ratios into practical rules for deciding when data belongs in memory, how large index pages should be, and how storage-system tradeoffs evolve with technology.
- [DBMSs on a Modern Processor: Where Does Time Go? (1999)](https://www.vldb.org/conf/1999/P28.pdf): A careful measurement study that explains why sophisticated processors often fail to accelerate DBMS workloads proportionally, grounding later hardware-conscious database design in instruction, cache, and branch behavior.
- [Database Architecture Optimized for the New Bottleneck: Memory Access (1999)](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/11189/): A foundational hardware-conscious database paper that identifies memory latency as the new bottleneck and turns that diagnosis into vertically partitioned storage and cache-efficient radix join algorithms.
- ["One Size Fits All": An Idea Whose Time Has Come and Gone (2005)](https://cs.brown.edu/people/ugur/fits_all.pdf): The manifesto that launched Stonebraker's 'specialized engines' era, arguing that the generic DBMS architecture isn't optimal for data warehousing, streaming, or scientific data — a direct motivation for C-Store and H-Store.
- [Architecture of a Database System (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1561/1900000002): A survey-style tour of how a DBMS is actually built end to end — process models, storage, buffer management, concurrency control, and query processing — connecting decades of research into one coherent picture.
- [Database Cracking (2007)](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2007/papers/cidr07p07.pdf): Introduces adaptive indexing as a side effect of query processing, letting physical organization evolve continuously with the workload instead of requiring an up-front tuning decision.
- [MonetDB: Two Decades of Research in Column-oriented Database Architectures (2012)](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/19929): A compact architectural history of MonetDB that connects columnar storage, CPU-conscious execution, adaptive indexing, run-time optimization, and modular system design across two decades of CWI research.
- [Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2012.33): Refines the CAP theorem — even without a partition, there's a trade-off between latency and consistency (PACELC).
- [Umbra: A Disk-Based System with In-Memory Performance (2020)](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2020/papers/p29-neumann-cidr20.pdf): Explains Umbra's evolution beyond pure in-memory HyPer, including a low-overhead buffer manager with variable-size pages that preserves cached performance while scaling gracefully to SSD-resident data.

### Database History

- [A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (1970)](https://doi.org/10.1145/362384.362685): Establishes the relational model and its separation of logical data relationships from physical representation, providing the intellectual starting point for modern relational databases.
- [Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1145/582095.582099): The origin of cost-based query optimization; the template for practically every relational optimizer since.
- [What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around... (2024)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3685980.3685986): A tour of six decades of data-model history — hierarchical, relational, object-oriented, XML, NoSQL, and now vector/AI-native — arguing the same ideas keep resurfacing and asking what's genuinely new versus recycled.

### Deterministic Databases

- [Calvin: Fast Distributed Transactions for Partitioned Database Systems (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2213836.2213838): Makes distributed transactions cheap by agreeing on a deterministic execution order for a batch up front, so replicas execute independently and stay consistent without per-transaction coordination.
- [An Overview of Deterministic Database Systems (2018)](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-cacm2018.pdf): A synthesis article explaining the deterministic paradigm (the basis of Calvin) as an alternative to classical serializability — instead of discovering a serial order at runtime, the system fixes it in advance.
- [SLOG: Serializable, Low-Latency, Geo-Replicated Transactions (2019)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol12/p1747-ren.pdf): Extends Calvin's deterministic approach to exploit data locality across geo-replicated regions, achieving strictly serializable transactions with an order of magnitude lower latency than Spanner/Calvin for workloads with regional locality.
- [Aria: A Fast and Practical Deterministic OLTP Database (2020)](https://doi.org/10.14778/3407790.3407808): Uses deterministic batch execution with lightweight dependency checks to avoid locking and distributed commit overhead while retaining practical OLTP performance.
- [Detock: High Performance Multi-Region Transactions at Scale (2023)](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/detock-umd.pdf): The most recent entry in Abadi's deterministic-database lineage (after Calvin and SLOG), handling strictly serializable multi-region transactions with almost no performance degradation even under very high conflict rates.

### Distributed Systems Testing

- [Lineage-Driven Fault Injection (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2723372.2723711): Uses data lineage to target only failures capable of changing an application's outcome, replacing combinatorial fault exploration with focused experiments.
- [FoundationDB: A Distributed Unbundled Transactional Key Value Store (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3448016.3457559): An unbundled transactional key-value store, famous for its deterministic simulation testing — a bridge to distributed-systems testing.
- [Feedback-guided Adaptive Testing of Distributed Systems Designs (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi26/presentation/li): A modern read on combining feedback-guided exploration and formal models to find distributed-systems bugs.
- [Pilot Execution: Simulating Failure Recovery In Situ for Distributed Systems (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi26/presentation/li-zhenyu): Focuses on the recovery path, traditionally hard to test, and demonstrates the technique across several large-scale distributed systems.
- [Themis: Detecting Distributed Concurrency Bugs through RPC-Driven Race-Directed Test Generation and Fuzzing (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi26/presentation/cao): Combines static analysis, LLM-assisted test generation, and directed fuzzing to find concurrency bugs in real systems.

### Distributed Storage

- [Eventually-Serializable Data Services (1996)](https://doi.org/10.1145/248052.248113): An early formal model for replicated services that guarantee only eventual serializability, letting clients get fast local responses while a background process reconciles operation order.
- [The Google File System (2003)](https://doi.org/10.1145/945445.945450): A chunk-based distributed file system for huge, append-mostly files, built around a single metadata master and relaxed consistency — the storage layer that made MapReduce and Bigtable possible.
- [Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (2006)](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/osdi06/tech/chang.html): A sparse, distributed, sorted multi-dimensional map (row, column family, timestamp) built on GFS and Chubby, giving Google one wide-column store for workloads from crawled pages to real-time serving.
- [Ceph: A Scalable, High-Performance Distributed File System (2006)](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/osdi06/tech/weil.html): Uses the CRUSH algorithm to let clients compute data placement instead of looking it up, removing a central directory bottleneck while still surviving failures and rebalancing automatically.
- [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (2007)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1323293.1294281): The seminal paper on Dynamo's architecture — consistent hashing, sloppy quorums, vector clocks, gossip, and availability as an explicit design priority.
- [PNUTS: Yahoo!'s Hosted Data Serving Platform (2008)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.14778/1454159.1454167): Yahoo!'s geographically distributed record store for web-scale serving, offering per-record timeline consistency instead of full serializability — a foundational "NoSQL era" paper alongside Dynamo and Bigtable.
- [RAMCloud: Scalable High-Performance Storage Entirely in DRAM (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2043556.2043558): Reconsiders distributed storage around cluster-wide DRAM and shows how fast crash recovery can make volatile primary storage practical.
- [On Brewing Fresh Espresso: LinkedIn's Distributed Data Serving Platform (2013)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2463676.2465298): LinkedIn's distributed, document-oriented OLTP store, with transactional multi-document updates, real-time secondary indexing, and a change-capture stream — a bridge between the NoSQL era and the later NewSQL wave.
- [TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph (2013)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc13/technical-sessions/presentation/bronson): A graph-aware caching layer in front of MySQL serving Facebook's social graph, with read-after-write consistency per region and eventual consistency across regions — tuned for a read-to-write ratio in the hundreds.
- [Adapting to Access Locality via Live Data Migration in Globally Distributed Datastores (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1109/BigData.2018.8622565): Defines practical requirements for moving live data toward changing demand while preserving availability, load balance, and low access latency.
- [Amazon DynamoDB: A Scalable, Predictably Performant, and Fully Managed NoSQL Database Service (2022)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc22/presentation/elhemali): Shows how Dynamo's ideas evolved into a fully managed, multi-tenant service with strict scale and predictability goals.
- [WriteGuards: Distributed Storage Support for Strongly Consistent Caches (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/technical-sessions): Reopens a classic problem — strongly consistent caching — with a lightweight storage primitive, evaluated on TiDB.

### Distributed Training

- [Large Scale Distributed Deep Networks (2012)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2012/hash/6aca97005c68f1206823815f66102863-Abstract.html): Introduces the DistBelief architecture and Downpour SGD, establishing core patterns for training neural networks across large compute clusters.
- [Scaling Distributed Machine Learning with the Parameter Server (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2640087.2644155): A distributed key-value abstraction for sharding and asynchronously synchronizing model parameters across machines, letting training scale to models and datasets too large for one machine's memory or bandwidth.
- [TensorFlow: A System for Large-Scale Machine Learning (2016)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi16/technical-sessions/presentation/abadi): Represents ML computations as dataflow graphs that can be partitioned and scheduled across CPUs, GPUs, and distributed clusters with the same program, unifying research prototyping and production deployment.
- [Horovod: Fast and Easy Distributed Deep Learning in TensorFlow (2018)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc18/presentation/sergeev): Distributed training via ring all-reduce, simple to adopt; a good entry point into collective communication for ML.
- [Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053): Tensor parallelism for training transformers with billions of parameters; the basis of the modern LLM-training stack.
- [PipeDream: Generalized Pipeline Parallelism for DNN Training (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3341301.3359646): Pipeline parallelism with scheduling that keeps GPUs busy; a central piece of large-scale training.
- [Salus: Fine-Grained GPU Sharing Primitives for Deep Learning Applications (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04610): Introduces fast iteration-level GPU sharing and memory-lane primitives that let training jobs coexist without the overhead of process-level time slicing.
- [Pollux: Co-adaptive Cluster Scheduling for Goodput-Optimized Deep Learning (2021)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi21/presentation/qiao): Schedules DL training by optimizing 'goodput,' jointly adjusting resources and batch size. A direct heir to Gandiva.
- [Youmu: Efficient Columnar Data Pipeline for LLM Training (2025)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2025): A good recent example of the convergence between columnar data engineering and LLM training pipelines.
- [Di-PS: System-Algorithm Co-Design for Asynchronous and Resilient Cross-Cluster LLM Training (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi26/presentation/li-shengwei): Updates the parameter-server idea for LLM training across heterogeneous, geographically separated clusters.
- [Efficient Long-Context Language Model Training by Core Attention Disaggregation (2026)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2026/hash/423b59ae02381f27862c21d1c41a5603-Abstract-Conference.html): Explores disaggregation not in serving but within long-context LLM training, isolating core attention as a specialized resource.

### Distributed Transactions

- [Life Beyond Distributed Transactions: An Apostate's Opinion (2007)](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2007/papers/cidr07p15.pdf): A provocative essay on designing systems that avoid distributed transactions. Sparks discussion even in a small group.
- [Megastore: Providing Scalable, Highly Available Storage for Interactive Services (2011)](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2011/Papers/CIDR11_Paper32.pdf): Layers semi-relational schemas and synchronous, Paxos-replicated transactions over Bigtable, partitioning data into small 'entity groups' to keep cross-group transactions rare and cheap.
- [Calvin: Fast Distributed Transactions for Partitioned Database Systems (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2213836.2213838): Makes distributed transactions cheap by agreeing on a deterministic execution order for a batch up front, so replicas execute independently and stay consistent without per-transaction coordination.
- [F1 - The Fault-Tolerant Distributed RDBMS Supporting Google's Ad Business (2012)](https://research.google/pubs/f1-the-fault-tolerant-distributed-rdbms-supporting-googles-ad-business/): The first F1 system paper describes Google's migration of core advertising services from MySQL to a fault-tolerant, strongly consistent distributed RDBMS, including the application and schema changes used to absorb wide-area transaction latency.
- [Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2012.33): Refines the CAP theorem — even without a partition, there's a trade-off between latency and consistency (PACELC).
- [Probabilistically Bounded Staleness for Practical Partial Quorums (2012)](https://doi.org/10.14778/2212351.2212359): Quantifies, in closed form, how stale a partial-quorum read is likely to be — explaining why Dynamo-style quorums are usually "good enough" in practice despite no worst-case guarantee.
- [The Potential Dangers of Causal Consistency and an Explicit Solution (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2391229.2391251): Shows that classic causal consistency's dependency tracking scales poorly, and proposes narrowing to application-defined "explicit causality" instead of full potential causality.
- [Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database (2012)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi12/technical-sessions/presentation/corbett): Uses TrueTime — GPS and atomic clocks bounding clock uncertainty — to assign globally meaningful commit timestamps, giving externally consistent transactions across datacenters without a central coordinator.
- [Bolt-on Causal Consistency (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2463676.2465279): Turns explicit causality into a practical "bolt-on" shim that upgrades any eventually consistent store to convergent causal consistency without modifying the store itself.
- [F1: A Distributed SQL Database That Scales (2013)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol6/p1068-shute.pdf): Layers a distributed SQL query engine and a familiar relational schema on top of Spanner's storage, showing how Google rebuilt strong consistency and SQL semantics for AdWords after leaving sharded MySQL.
- [Online, Asynchronous Schema Change in F1 (2013)](https://research.google/pubs/online-asynchronous-schema-change-in-f1/): Formalizes safe schema evolution for a globally distributed database whose stateless servers adopt versions asynchronously, then shows how F1 decomposes dangerous changes into corruption-free transitions while remaining online.
- [HAT, not CAP: Towards Highly Available Transactions (2013)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/hotos13/session/bailis): The HotOS position paper that first argues for classifying transactional guarantees by whether they require coordination under partition, setting up the taxonomy the VLDB '14 paper formalizes.
- [Hekaton: SQL Server's Memory-Optimized OLTP Engine (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2463676.2463710): In-memory OLTP inside a commercial DBMS — lock-free latches and stored-procedure compilation.
- [Highly Available Transactions: Virtues and Limitations (2014)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol7/p181-bailis.pdf): Formally defines the transactional guarantees achievable without sacrificing availability under the CAP trade-off, showing which isolation levels are compatible with high availability.
- [Scalable Atomic Visibility with RAMP Transactions (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2588555.2588562): Provides atomic visibility across partitions using only limited multi-versioning and client-side repair, avoiding coordination entirely and scaling linearly where classic 2PC does not.
- [Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems (2015)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p185-bailis.pdf): Introduces 'invariant confluence,' a formal criterion for knowing when an application invariant can be maintained without coordination between nodes — generalizes the HAT line of work into a broader theory of when coordination is actually necessary.
- [No Compromises: Distributed Transactions with Consistency, Availability, and Performance (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2815400.2815425): Fast distributed transactions over RDMA; shows what changes once the network stops being the bottleneck.
- [Panopticon: A Lock Broker Architecture for Scalable Transactions in the Datacenter (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1109/BigData.2015.7363762): Revisits centralized locking with a scalable broker design, showing when strong coordination can outperform more fragmented transaction management.
- [Building Consistent Transactions with Inconsistent Replication (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2815400.2815404): Co-designs replication and transaction processing so that strong transactional guarantees do not require consensus on every operation.
- [Spanner: Becoming a SQL System (2017)](https://research.google/pubs/spanner-becoming-a-sql-system/): The database-focused Spanner follow-up explains how a globally distributed key-value system evolved into relational SQL, including query routing and execution during resharding, transient-failure restarts, range extraction, and blockwise-columnar storage.
- [Spanner, TrueTime and the CAP Theorem (2017)](https://research.google/pubs/spanner-truetime-and-the-cap-theorem/): A concise clarification of how Spanner combines strong consistency with high availability without contradicting CAP, and of TrueTime's specific role in externally consistent transactions and snapshot reads.
- [An Overview of Deterministic Database Systems (2018)](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-cacm2018.pdf): A synthesis article explaining the deterministic paradigm (the basis of Calvin) as an alternative to classical serializability — instead of discovering a serial order at runtime, the system fixes it in advance.
- [F1 Query: Declarative Querying at Scale (2018)](https://research.google/pubs/f1-query-declarative-querying-at-scale/): The key F1 follow-on for query processing, describing a production federated SQL platform that spans files and storage systems while supporting point queries, interactive analytics, and large ETL pipelines.
- [SLOG: Serializable, Low-Latency, Geo-Replicated Transactions (2019)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol12/p1747-ren.pdf): Extends Calvin's deterministic approach to exploit data locality across geo-replicated regions, achieving strictly serializable transactions with an order of magnitude lower latency than Spanner/Calvin for workloads with regional locality.
- [F1 Lightning: HTAP as a Service (2020)](https://research.google/pubs/f1-lightning-htap-as-a-service/): A production HTAP case study for brownfield environments, showing how Google added fast analytical access across existing transactional systems without requiring the query service to own or replace them.
- [FoundationDB: A Distributed Unbundled Transactional Key Value Store (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3448016.3457559): An unbundled transactional key-value store, famous for its deterministic simulation testing — a bridge to distributed-systems testing.
- [Detock: High Performance Multi-Region Transactions at Scale (2023)](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/detock-umd.pdf): The most recent entry in Abadi's deterministic-database lineage (after Calvin and SLOG), handling strictly serializable multi-region transactions with almost no performance degradation even under very high conflict rates.
- [Distributed Transactions at Scale in Amazon DynamoDB (2023)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc23/presentation/idziorek): Complements the DynamoDB paper by explaining how the service offers distributed ACID transactions without giving up its scale and availability requirements.
- [Design and Modular Verification of Distributed Transactions in MongoDB (2025)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p5045-schultz.pdf): Shows how modular formal specifications and model-based tests can validate the subtle boundary between MongoDB's distributed transaction protocol and its WiredTiger storage engine.

### Dynamo Family

- [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (2007)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1323293.1294281): The seminal paper on Dynamo's architecture — consistent hashing, sloppy quorums, vector clocks, gossip, and availability as an explicit design priority.
- [Eventually Consistent (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1435417.1435432): A practitioner's tour of the consistency spectrum between strong and eventual, and of the client-side guarantees that make weak consistency usable at Amazon scale.
- [Cassandra: A Decentralized Structured Storage System (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1773912.1773922): Combines Bigtable's data model with Dynamo's eventually-consistent, peer-to-peer replication — built at Facebook for an inbox-search workload that needed wide-column flexibility with no single point of failure.
- [Dotted Version Vectors: Logical Clocks for Optimistic Replication (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.5808): Shows why server-id and client-id version vectors either lose causality or grow without bound, and introduces dotted version vectors as an exact clock sized by the replication degree.
- [Scalable and Accurate Causality Tracking for Eventually Consistent Stores (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-43352-2_6): Gives the full treatment of dotted version vectors and introduces DVV sets, a compact per-key clock for all siblings, together with a small kernel of operations any key-value store clock must implement.
- [Amazon DynamoDB: A Scalable, Predictably Performant, and Fully Managed NoSQL Database Service (2022)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc22/presentation/elhemali): Shows how Dynamo's ideas evolved into a fully managed, multi-tenant service with strict scale and predictability goals.
- [Trie Memtables in Cassandra (2022)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.14778/3554821.3554828): Replaces Cassandra's skip-list partition map with sharded byte-comparable tries, shrinking heap pressure while accelerating reads and writes.
- [Distributed Transactions at Scale in Amazon DynamoDB (2023)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc23/presentation/idziorek): Complements the DynamoDB paper by explaining how the service offers distributed ACID transactions without giving up its scale and availability requirements.

### Fault Tolerance Bft

- [The Byzantine Generals Problem (1982)](https://doi.org/10.1145/357172.357176): Formalizes reaching agreement when some participants may lie or act arbitrarily rather than just fail silently, and proves how many honest participants are needed to tolerate a given number of traitors.
- [Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (1999)](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/osdi99/full_papers/castro/castro.pdf): The first BFT protocol practical enough for real systems; the basis for much of the later work on Byzantine fault tolerance.
- [Zyzzyva: Speculative Byzantine Fault Tolerance (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1294261.1294267): Shows how speculative execution can reduce the normal-case cost of Byzantine replication while retaining a recovery path for faults and conflicts.
- [HotStuff: BFT Consensus with Linearity and Responsiveness (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3293611.3331591): Builds a responsive BFT protocol with linear leader communication and a simple view-change structure that strongly influenced modern replicated ledgers.
- [BunchBFT: Across-Cluster Consensus Protocol (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10658): Explores a hierarchical, cluster-based BFT design that reduces wide-area communication costs while retaining consensus safety and liveness.
- [Pilot Execution: Simulating Failure Recovery In Situ for Distributed Systems (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi26/presentation/li-zhenyu): Focuses on the recovery path, traditionally hard to test, and demonstrates the technique across several large-scale distributed systems.

### Isolation Concurrency

- [Granularity of Locks and Degrees of Consistency in a Shared Data Base (1976)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1282480.1282513): Defines lock granularity and degrees of consistency — vocabulary still used for isolation levels today.
- [A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels (1995)](https://doi.org/10.1145/223784.223785): Shows the ANSI SQL isolation-level definitions, based on forbidding specific phenomena, are ambiguous and don't characterize what commercial databases actually implement — motivating later serializability-graph-based definitions.
- [Generalized Isolation Level Definitions (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDE.2000.839388): Replaces ANSI SQL's informal, phenomenon-based isolation definitions with precise ones based on dependency graphs, finally giving snapshot isolation and other multiversion levels a rigorous specification.
- [A Read-Only Transaction Anomaly Under Snapshot Isolation (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1031570.1031573): The short note identifying that even a read-only transaction can trigger a serialization anomaly under Snapshot Isolation, motivating the theory behind "Making Snapshot Isolation Serializable."
- [Allocating Isolation Levels to Transactions (2005)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1065167.1065193): Fekete's solo work showing how to guarantee serializable execution by mixing isolation levels — some transactions ('pivots') running under 2PL and the rest under Snapshot Isolation — without requiring the whole system to pay the cost of full serializability.
- [Making Snapshot Isolation Serializable (2005)](https://dsf.berkeley.edu/cs286/papers/ssi-tods2005.pdf): Characterizes exactly when Snapshot Isolation produces non-serializable histories and shows how to detect these anomalies — the direct theoretical ancestor of the Serializable Snapshot Isolation implemented in PostgreSQL.
- [Serializable Isolation for Snapshot Databases (2008)](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~kubitron/courses/cs262a-F13/handouts/papers/p729-cahill.pdf): Describes the runtime algorithm that automatically detects and prevents Snapshot Isolation anomalies — it's this algorithm, not the 2005 theory paper, that ended up implemented as Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL.
- [Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL (2012)](https://doi.org/10.14778/2367502.2367523): Turns serializable snapshot isolation into a production PostgreSQL feature through practical detection of dangerous dependency structures.
- [Speedy Transactions in Multicore In-Memory Databases (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2517349.2522713): An in-memory OCC engine that avoids the centralized commit-sequence counter that bottlenecked prior designs, using epoch-based timestamps to scale near-linearly across many cores.
- [Staring into the Abyss: An Evaluation of Concurrency Control with One Thousand Cores (2014)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p209-yu.pdf): A rigorous evaluation of seven classic concurrency-control protocols simulated up to 1,000 cores, showing that all of them hit scalability walls — explains the design pressures behind systems like Silo and Hekaton.
- [Rethinking Serializable Multiversion Concurrency Control (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.2324): Proposes Bohm, an MVCC protocol for in-memory databases that guarantees serializability without ever blocking reads behind concurrent writes, decoupling version assignment from transaction execution.
- [Feral Concurrency Control: An Empirical Investigation of Modern Application Integrity (2015)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2723372.2737784): An empirical study showing that most real applications (Rails, Django, etc.) use 'feral,' application-level integrity mechanisms instead of the database's own concurrency control — a practical counterpoint to formal isolation guarantees.
- [TicToc: Time Traveling Optimistic Concurrency Control (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2882903.2882935): Decouples logical transaction time from physical execution order, reducing aborts while retaining serializability in multicore in-memory databases.

### Kv Cache Management

- [Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02150): Introduces multi-query attention, sharing a single key/value head across all query heads to cut the memory-bandwidth cost of loading KV state during autoregressive decoding.
- [GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints (2023)](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.298/): Interpolates between multi-head and multi-query attention, letting existing checkpoints be uptrained into a grouped-query form that shrinks the KV cache with little quality loss.
- [H₂O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models (2023)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/6ceefa7b15572587b78ecfcebb2827f8-Abstract-Conference.html): Shows that a small, dynamically identified subset of tokens dominates attention scores, letting most of the KV cache be evicted without hurting generation quality.
- [CacheGen: KV Cache Compression and Streaming for Fast Large Language Model Serving (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3651890.3672274): Treats cached context as networked state, encoding KV tensors so precomputed prefixes can be streamed across machines and storage tiers far faster than recomputing them.
- [KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache (2024)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/liu24bz.html): Shows that keys and values have different outlier distributions and quantizes each asymmetrically to 2 bits without fine-tuning, cutting peak memory while preserving quality.
- [PyramidKV: Dynamic KV Cache Compression based on Pyramidal Information Funneling (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02069): Observes that attention narrows from broad to focused across layers and allocates a shrinking KV cache budget per layer instead of a uniform one, retaining full-cache accuracy at a fraction of the memory.
- [SnapKV: LLM Knows What You Are Looking for Before Generation (2024)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/28ab418242603e0f7323e54185d19bde-Abstract-Conference.html): Observes that attention heads consistently focus on the same prompt positions and uses that pattern to compress the KV cache before generation even starts.
- [Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks (2024)](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/5e5fd18f863cbe6d8ae392a93fd271c9-Abstract-Conference.html): Explains why naively evicting old KV entries breaks windowed attention and shows that keeping a handful of initial "sink" tokens lets bounded caches support effectively unbounded streams.
- [Mooncake: Trading More Storage for Less Computation — A KVCache-centric Architecture for Serving LLM Chatbot (2025)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast25/presentation/qin): Builds a distributed KV cache spanning GPU memory, CPU DRAM, SSD and the network across separate prefill/decode clusters, treating cache placement as a first-class distributed-storage problem.

### Lakehouse

- [Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores (2020)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p3411-armbrust.pdf): Adds a transaction log on top of Parquet files in object storage to give data lakes ACID guarantees, schema enforcement, and time travel, without requiring a dedicated warehouse to hold the data.
- [Apache Hudi: The Streaming Data Lake Platform (2021)](https://hudi.apache.org/blog/2021/07/21/streaming-data-lake-platform/): Presents Hudi's approach to mutable data lakes through incremental ingestion, indexing, compaction, and table services rather than append-only batch replacement.
- [Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms that Unify Data Warehousing and Advanced Analytics (2021)](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2021/papers/cidr2021_paper17.pdf): Argues that adding DBMS-style management and performance features (indexing, caching, ACID) directly on open data-lake file formats collapses the traditional warehouse-plus-lake architecture into one system.

### Learned Indexes

- [The Case for Learned Index Structures (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3183713.3196909): What if database indexes were learned models? Opened the agenda of applying ML to database components.
- [DILI: A Distribution-Driven Learned Index (2023)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol16/p2212-li.pdf): Builds an update-capable learned tree whose fanout and leaf models follow local key distributions, balancing model accuracy against traversal depth.
- [Algorithmic Complexity Attacks on Dynamic Learned Indexes (2023)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p780-yang.pdf): Shows how carefully chosen inserts can drive a dynamic learned index into extreme memory use or thousand-fold slowdowns, making worst-case robustness part of index design.
- [Learned Index: A Comprehensive Experimental Evaluation (2023)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol16/p1992-li.pdf): Tests learned and traditional indexes under one framework, exposing where model-based designs help and where updates, strings, concurrency, and range scans erase their advantage.
- [Making In-Memory Learned Indexes Efficient on Disk (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3654954): Derives six storage-aware transformations that turn memory-first learned indexes into disk layouts that improve both throughput and space over B+ trees.
- [Accelerating String-key Learned Index Structures via Memoization-based Incremental Training (2024)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p1802-park.pdf): Reuses prior model-training work for updated string keys and offloads retraining to an FPGA, attacking the cost that makes mutable string learned indexes impractical.
- [Towards Systematic Index Dynamization (2024)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p2867-rumbaugh.pdf): Turns specialized static indexes into update-capable structures through a configurable dynamization framework, narrowing the gap from research prototype to deployable index.
- [DobLIX: A Dual-Objective Learned Index for Log-Structured Merge Trees (2025)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p3965-heidari.pdf): Co-optimizes learned-model accuracy and physical block access inside RocksDB, adapting its LSM index and data layout as workloads change.
- [FB+-tree: A Memory-Optimized B+-tree with Latch-Free Update (2025)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p1579-li.pdf): Blends trie-like byte-wise branching with a balanced B+ tree and latch-free updates to improve cache behavior and multicore scalability under contention.
- [Why Are Learned Indexes So Effective but Sometimes Ineffective? (2025)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p2886-liu.pdf): Reconciles the PGM-index's strong asymptotic bounds with memory-bound execution in practice, then uses that diagnosis to build the faster PGM++.

### LLM Serving

- [Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models (2022)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu): Introduces iteration-level (continuous) batching for transformer inference — scheduling new requests into a batch as soon as any sequence finishes, instead of waiting for the whole batch — dramatically raising LLM-serving throughput.
- [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165): Manages the KV cache like an OS manages virtual memory, paging it into non-contiguous blocks, nearly eliminating the memory fragmentation that previously limited how many LLM requests could be served concurrently.
- [CacheGen: KV Cache Compression and Streaming for Fast Large Language Model Serving (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3651890.3672274): Treats cached context as networked state, encoding KV tensors so precomputed prefixes can be streamed across machines and storage tiers far faster than recomputing them.
- [DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-Optimized Large Language Model Serving (2024)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi24/presentation/zhong-yinmin): Separates prefill and decoding onto independently provisioned GPU pools to remove interference and optimize serving capacity under distinct latency objectives.
- [SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104): Co-designs a language and runtime for multi-call model programs, using prefix-aware KV-cache reuse and optimized structured decoding to raise throughput.
- [Mooncake: Trading More Storage for Less Computation — A KVCache-centric Architecture for Serving LLM Chatbot (2025)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast25/presentation/qin): Builds a distributed KV cache spanning GPU memory, CPU DRAM, SSD and the network across separate prefill/decode clusters, treating cache placement as a first-class distributed-storage problem.
- [SOLA: Optimizing SLO Attainment for Large Language Model Serving with State-Aware Scheduling (2025)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2025): Represents the post-vLLM generation of schedulers that treat state and SLOs as central elements of serving.
- [ThunderServe: High-performance and Cost-efficient LLM Serving in Cloud Environments (2025)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/c2a0e26dd9ee7d57e92bb1c24b39659a-Abstract-Conference.html): Explores LLM serving across heterogeneous clouds and makes cost, network, and placement an explicit part of the optimization.
- [Efficient LLM Serving on Commodity GPU Clusters with Data-Reduced Cross-Instance Orchestration (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/technical-sessions): Shows how to adapt prefill/decode disaggregation to clusters without cutting-edge interconnects, a relevant constraint outside hyperscalers.
- [Prism: Cost-Efficient Multi-LLM Serving via GPU Memory Ballooning (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/technical-sessions): Turns multi-model serving into an explicit problem of dynamic memory management and GPU efficiency.
- [SuperInfer: SLO-Aware Rotary Scheduling and Memory Management for LLM Inference on Superchips (2026)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2026): Represents the recent specialization of inference schedulers for new accelerator and memory topologies.

### LLM Training

- [Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053): Tensor parallelism for training transformers with billions of parameters; the basis of the modern LLM-training stack.
- [PipeDream: Generalized Pipeline Parallelism for DNN Training (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3341301.3359646): Pipeline parallelism with scheduling that keeps GPUs busy; a central piece of large-scale training.
- [Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16668): Couples conditional computation with compiler-managed sharding to train sparse models containing hundreds of billions of parameters across accelerator meshes.
- [ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1109/SC41405.2020.00024): Eliminates the memory redundancy of standard data parallelism by partitioning optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across GPUs instead of replicating them on every device, enabling trillion-parameter models without model parallelism.
- [Alpa: Automating Inter- and Intra-Operator Parallelism for Distributed Deep Learning (2022)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/zheng-lianmin): Automatically searches for a combination of inter-operator (pipeline) and intra-operator (tensor) parallelism strategies, instead of requiring engineers to hand-design the parallelization plan for each new large model.
- [Di-PS: System-Algorithm Co-Design for Asynchronous and Resilient Cross-Cluster LLM Training (2026)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi26/presentation/li-shengwei): Updates the parameter-server idea for LLM training across heterogeneous, geographically separated clusters.
- [Efficient Long-Context Language Model Training by Core Attention Disaggregation (2026)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2026/hash/423b59ae02381f27862c21d1c41a5603-Abstract-Conference.html): Explores disaggregation not in serving but within long-context LLM training, isolating core attention as a specialized resource.

### Logical Time Consensus

- [Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System (1978)](https://doi.org/10.1145/359545.359563): Shows that in a distributed system with no shared clock, you can still define a consistent 'happens-before' partial order using logical clocks — the foundation nearly every later consistency and consensus protocol builds on.
- [Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3149.214121): Proves no fully asynchronous consensus protocol can guarantee both safety and termination if even one process might fail — the impossibility result every practical protocol like Paxos or Raft has to work around.
- [Logical Physical Clocks (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-14472-6_2): Combines causal ordering with timestamps close to physical time, making logical-clock guarantees practical for snapshots and transactions in distributed databases.
- [Why Logical Clocks Are Easy (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2890782): Derives causal histories, vector clocks, version vectors, and dotted version vectors from one idea, tracking the set of events that precede each event, so the update rules follow from it.

### Membership Gossip

- [Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-peer Lookup Service for Internet Applications (2001)](https://doi.org/10.1145/383059.383071): The canonical DHT; its consistent hashing and ring routing reappear in Dynamo and Cassandra.
- [SWIM: Scalable Weakly-consistent Infection-style Process Group Membership Protocol (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1109/DSN.2002.1028914): A gossip-based failure detector that decouples detection speed from cluster size using randomized indirect probing, keeping per-node message load constant as the cluster grows.
- [Kelips: Building an Efficient and Stable P2P DHT Through Increased Memory and Background Overhead (2003)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-45172-3_15): A DHT that trades some memory for O(1) lookups by replicating routing state via gossip, instead of the O(log n) hops typical of Chord-style rings.
- [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (2007)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1323293.1294281): The seminal paper on Dynamo's architecture — consistent hashing, sloppy quorums, vector clocks, gossip, and availability as an explicit design priority.
