- [Lifeguard: Local Health Awareness for More Accurate Failure Detection (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1109/DSN-W.2018.00017): Hardens SWIM-style membership against false positives caused by locally overloaded nodes by making failure detection aware of each participant's health.

### Memory Efficient Search Structures

- [Modern B-Tree Techniques (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1561/1900000028): A comprehensive reference that goes far beyond textbook B-trees to cover transactional techniques, recovery, bulk and online utilities, advanced key structures, hardware effects, and robust query-processing uses.
- [The Adaptive Radix Tree: ARTful Indexing for Main-Memory Databases (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDE.2013.6544812): Introduces a radix tree whose node representation adapts to local fanout, combining cache-efficient point lookups with ordered scans and compact memory use.
- [HOT: A Height Optimized Trie Index for Main-Memory Database Systems (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3183713.3196896): Varies the number of discriminating bits per trie node to retain high fanout, low height, and compact SIMD-friendly search for sparse string keys.
- [SuRF: Practical Range Query Filtering with Fast Succinct Tries (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3183713.3196931): Extends approximate filtering beyond point membership by encoding an ordered key set as a compact trie that can reject empty range queries before storage access.
- [Order-Preserving Key Compression for In-Memory Search Trees (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3318464.3380583): Compresses variable-length keys without changing their sort order, allowing existing tries and B-trees to use less memory while continuing to compare encoded keys directly.
- [Memory-Efficient Search Trees for Database Management Systems (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3448016.3461470): Synthesizes succinct static trees, update-friendly hybrid indexing, and order-preserving compression into a unified account of reducing DBMS index memory.
- [DILI: A Distribution-Driven Learned Index (2023)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol16/p2212-li.pdf): Builds an update-capable learned tree whose fanout and leaf models follow local key distributions, balancing model accuracy against traversal depth.
- [Memento Filter: A Fast, Dynamic, and Robust Range Filter (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3698820): Makes range filtering dynamic and workload-robust, extending the idea beyond static LSM components to changing B-tree indexes such as WiredTiger.
- [Accelerating String-key Learned Index Structures via Memoization-based Incremental Training (2024)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p1802-park.pdf): Reuses prior model-training work for updated string keys and offloads retraining to an FPGA, attacking the cost that makes mutable string learned indexes impractical.
- [Towards Systematic Index Dynamization (2024)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p2867-rumbaugh.pdf): Turns specialized static indexes into update-capable structures through a configurable dynamization framework, narrowing the gap from research prototype to deployable index.
- [FB+-tree: A Memory-Optimized B+-tree with Latch-Free Update (2025)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p1579-li.pdf): Blends trie-like byte-wise branching with a balanced B+ tree and latch-free updates to improve cache behavior and multicore scalability under contention.

### Metastable Failures

- [Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems (2021)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3458336.3465286): Names and frames a failure pattern — a self-sustaining collapse that persists even after the trigger that caused it is gone — that had been recurring in production outages for years without a shared vocabulary.
- [Metastable Failures in the Wild (2022)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/huang-lexiang): A study of 22 real metastable incidents across 11 organizations, showing the pattern behind some of the most severe cloud outages of the last decade and the ad-hoc fixes operators reached for.
- [MSF-Model: Queuing-Based Analysis and Prediction of Metastable Failures in Replicated Storage Systems (2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10806504/): Turns metastability from a post-mortem narrative into a queuing model that predicts, before deployment, whether a given load and retry policy will trap a replicated store in a bad state.
- [Analyzing Metastable Failures (2025)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3713082.3730380): Argues that finding metastable-failure susceptibility by testing alone is hopeless given the size of the parameter space, and sketches what a principled, model-based search would need instead.
- [Formal Analysis of Metastable Failures in Software Systems (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03551): Delivers the formal treatment the HotOS position paper called for — modeling request-response systems as continuous-time Markov chains and predicting recovery behavior from escape probabilities in milliseconds.
- [Characterizing Metastable Faults and Failures (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00942): Reframes metastability around a causal mechanism — destabilizing cycles between individually well-behaved components — rather than the symptom-level framing the field started with, and tests it on three real case studies.

### ML Compilers

- [TVM: An Automated End-to-End Optimizing Compiler for Deep Learning (2018)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi18/presentation/chen): An end-to-end compiler that lowers high-level ML models to optimized code for very different hardware backends, using learned cost models to search the optimization space instead of hand-written per-target kernels.
- [Ansor: Generating High-Performance Tensor Programs for Deep Learning (2020)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/zheng): Expands tensor-program search beyond hand-written scheduling templates using hierarchical sampling, evolutionary search, and a learned cost model.

### ML Data Pipelines

- [TFX: A TensorFlow-Based Production-Scale Machine Learning Platform (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3097983.3098021): Google's production ML platform integrating training, validation, and serving; motivates replacing glue code with shared infrastructure.
- [Data Validation for Machine Learning (2019)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2019/hash/928f1160e52192e3e0017fb63ab65391-Abstract.html): Treats ML data as a production asset — detects anomalies, schema issues, and training/serving skew at petabyte scale. A strong read for anyone coming from databases.
- [tf.data: A Machine Learning Data Processing Framework (2021)](https://doi.org/10.14778/3476311.3476374): Defines composable ML input-pipeline operators and a runtime that overlaps, parallelizes, caches, and tunes data preparation for accelerator-fed training.
- [Youmu: Efficient Columnar Data Pipeline for LLM Training (2025)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2025): A good recent example of the convergence between columnar data engineering and LLM training pipelines.

### MLOps Production

- [Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2015/hash/86df7dcfd896fcaf2674f757a2463eba-Abstract.html): Catalogs the specific ways ML systems accumulate technical debt that traditional software doesn't — entanglement, hidden feedback loops, glue code, undeclared data dependencies — arguing most real-world ML code isn't the model.
- [TFX: A TensorFlow-Based Production-Scale Machine Learning Platform (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3097983.3098021): Google's production ML platform integrating training, validation, and serving; motivates replacing glue code with shared infrastructure.
- [Accelerating the Machine Learning Lifecycle with MLflow (2018)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/hotcloud18/presentation/zaharia): Experiment tracking, packaging, and model registry; became the de facto standard for the ML lifecycle.
- [Data Validation for Machine Learning (2019)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2019/hash/928f1160e52192e3e0017fb63ab65391-Abstract.html): Treats ML data as a production asset — detects anomalies, schema issues, and training/serving skew at petabyte scale. A strong read for anyone coming from databases.
- [ML Metadata: A Library for ML Experiments and Production (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.13283): Treats artifacts, executions, and lineage as structured metadata so experiments and production ML pipelines can be tracked and reproduced.
- [PROMPTS: PeRformance Optimization via Multi-Agent Planning for LLM Training and Serving (2026)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2026/hash/48253da5351effdfea994fd7bbff7005-Abstract-Conference.html): A recent example of AI being used to optimize its own training and serving infrastructure.

### Model Serving

- [Clipper: A Low-Latency Online Prediction Serving System (2017)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi17/technical-sessions/presentation/crankshaw): Sits between trained models and applications as a model-agnostic serving layer, using adaptive batching and caching to hit latency targets regardless of which ML framework produced the model.
- [Serving DNNs Like Clockwork: Performance Predictability from the Bottom Up (2020)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/gujarati): Builds predictable model serving from deterministic GPU execution, supporting thousands of models while meeting strict request-level latency objectives.

### Modern Open Data Formats

- [Dremel: Interactive Analysis of Web-Scale Datasets (2010)](https://doi.org/10.14778/1920841.1920886): Interactive queries over trillions of rows; the nested-data columnar storage that became the basis for BigQuery.
- [Data Blocks: Hybrid OLTP and OLAP on Compressed Storage using both Vectorization and Compilation (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2882903.2882925): Shows how a compressed block format can retain fast point access for transactions while supporting vectorized and compiled analytical execution over the same data.
- [Mainlining Databases: Supporting Fast Transactional Workloads on Universal Columnar Data File Formats (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14471): Explores how an OLTP engine can update Arrow-compatible columnar blocks directly, narrowing the divide between transactional storage and analytical interchange formats.
- [BtrBlocks: Efficient Columnar Compression for Data Lakes (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3589263): Reconsiders columnar compression for data lakes with an open format designed to decode and encode substantially faster than established Parquet implementations.
- [An Empirical Evaluation of Columnar Storage Formats (2023)](https://doi.org/10.14778/3626292.3626298): A component-level comparison of Parquet and ORC that exposes how their encodings, metadata, and compression choices behave on modern hardware and workloads.
- [Data Formats in Analytical DBMSs: Performance Trade-offs and Future Directions (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00778-025-00911-1): Compares Arrow, Parquet, and ORC as native analytical representations and identifies the trade-offs blocking a unified in-memory and on-disk format.
- [F3: The Open-Source Data File Format for the Future (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3749163): Proposes an extensible successor to Parquet and ORC that packages WebAssembly decoders with encoded data to preserve interoperability as encoding techniques evolve.
- [The FastLanes File Format (2025)](https://doi.org/10.14778/3749646.3749718): Designs a portable columnar format around composable encodings, fine-grained access, and layouts that decode efficiently on CPUs and GPUs.

### Observability And Telemetry

- [Characterizing User and Provider Reported Cloud Failures (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.12237): Compares three years of user-reported outages (via Down Detector) against providers' own incident reports, exposing how much cloud failure never makes it into an official post-mortem.
- [Fast Outage Analysis of Large-scale Production Clouds with Service Correlation Mining (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICSE43902.2021.00085): Mines correlations across a year of Azure production outages to automatically triage which service is the likely root cause, cutting the manual effort that normally bottlenecks incident response.

### OLTP Architecture

- [The End of an Architectural Era (It's Time for a Complete Rewrite) (2007)](https://www.vldb.org/conf/2007/papers/industrial/p1150-stonebraker.pdf): Argues with benchmark evidence that no single RDBMS architecture can be fast at everything, and sketches H-Store, a from-scratch, partitioned, in-memory OLTP design, as the alternative to retrofitting legacy code.
- [H-Store: A High-Performance, Distributed Main Memory Transaction Processing System (2008)](https://hstore.cs.brown.edu/papers/hstore-demo.pdf): The systems paper implementing the 'clean-slate' architecture argued for in 'The End of an Architectural Era' — partitioned, in-memory OLTP with stored procedures. A direct predecessor of VoltDB and of CMU's self-driving-database lineage.
- [OLTP Through the Looking Glass, and What We Found There (2008)](https://hstore.cs.brown.edu/papers/hstore-lookingglass.pdf): Breaks down exactly where a traditional OLTP DBMS spends its CPU cycles (logging, locking, latching, buffer management) and shows that less than 10% of the time is 'useful work' — the empirical evidence behind 'The End of an Architectural Era' and the design of H-Store.
- [HyPer: A Hybrid OLTP&OLAP Main Memory Database System Based on Virtual Memory Snapshots (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDE.2011.5767867): The defining HyPer system paper, showing how operating-system virtual-memory snapshots can isolate analytical scans from transactional updates while keeping both workloads on one in-memory database.
- [Hekaton: SQL Server's Memory-Optimized OLTP Engine (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2463676.2463710): In-memory OLTP inside a commercial DBMS — lock-free latches and stored-procedure compilation.
- [OLTP Through the Looking Glass 16 Years Later: Communication is the New Bottleneck (2025)](https://vldb.org/cidrdb/papers/2025/p17-zhou.pdf): Repeats the 2008 profiling exercise sixteen years later and finds a different culprit — communication, not logging/locking, now dominates CPU time in simple OLTP workloads like YCSB. The literal update, done by Stonebraker himself, of the original paper.

### Physical Hybrid Time

- [Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System (1978)](https://doi.org/10.1145/359545.359563): Shows that in a distributed system with no shared clock, you can still define a consistent 'happens-before' partial order using logical clocks — the foundation nearly every later consistency and consensus protocol builds on.
- [Maintaining the Time in a Distributed System (1983)](https://doi.org/10.1145/800221.806730): Represents each clock reading as an interval with an error bound and shows how servers combine intervals into a tighter, still-correct one, the idea TrueTime later exposes as an API.
- [Practical Uses of Synchronized Clocks in Distributed Systems (1991)](https://doi.org/10.1145/112600.112601): Shows how loosely synchronized clocks can replace message rounds in leases, at-most-once delivery, and cache consistency, as long as correctness never depends on the clocks staying in sync.
- [Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database (2012)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi12/technical-sessions/presentation/corbett): Uses TrueTime — GPS and atomic clocks bounding clock uncertainty — to assign globally meaningful commit timestamps, giving externally consistent transactions across datacenters without a central coordinator.
- [Beyond TrueTime: Using AugmentedTime for Improving Spanner (2013)](https://cse.buffalo.edu/~demirbas/publications/augmentedTime.pdf): Argues that TrueTime's commit wait and snapshot limits can be eased by also tracking causality inside the uncertainty window, an idea that leads directly to hybrid logical clocks.
- [Logical Physical Clocks (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-14472-6_2): Combines causal ordering with timestamps close to physical time, making logical-clock guarantees practical for snapshots and transactions in distributed databases.
- [Analysis of Bounds on Hybrid Vector Clocks (2015)](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.OPODIS.2015.34): Shows that hybrid vector clocks, which keep entries only for nodes heard from within the clock-uncertainty window, stay far smaller than full vector clocks in realistic settings.
- [Spanner, TrueTime and the CAP Theorem (2017)](https://research.google/pubs/spanner-truetime-and-the-cap-theorem/): A concise clarification of how Spanner combines strong consistency with high availability without contradicting CAP, and of TrueTime's specific role in externally consistent transactions and snapshot reads.
- [Exploiting a Natural Network Effect for Scalable, Fine-grained Clock Synchronization (2018)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi18/presentation/geng): Synchronizes datacenter clocks to within tens of nanoseconds in software by filtering noisy probes and using the network of clocks to correct each other's errors.
- [Implementation of Cluster-wide Logical Clock and Causal Consistency in MongoDB (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3299869.3314049): Describes how MongoDB runs a hybrid logical clock across a sharded cluster, signing cluster time so that clients cannot push it forward, to provide causally consistent sessions.
- [CockroachDB: The Resilient Geo-Distributed SQL Database (2020)](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/pdf/cockroachdb-the-resilient-geo-distributed-sql-database-sigmod-2020.pdf): Extends the Spanner lineage directly — Raft-replicated, horizontally-scalable SQL with serializable geo-distributed transactions — but without Spanner's specialized TrueTime hardware, using hybrid-logical clocks instead.
- [Sundial: Fault-tolerant Clock Synchronization for Datacenters (2020)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/li-yuliang): Keeps the clock-uncertainty bound near 100 ns even under link and device failures by detecting failures quickly in hardware and switching to a precomputed backup sync graph, and shows what that buys Spanner.

### Query Execution

- [Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1145/582095.582099): The origin of cost-based query optimization; the template for practically every relational optimizer since.
- [Encapsulation of Parallelism in the Volcano Query Processing System (1990)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/93605.98720): Introduces the exchange operator, which encapsulates process boundaries, communication, and flow control so ordinary query operators can gain intra-operator, pipelined, and bushy parallelism without being rewritten.
- [Query Evaluation Techniques for Large Databases (1993)](https://doi.org/10.1145/152610.152611): Graefe's landmark survey unifies the implementation principles behind iterators, sorting, hashing, set-matching, complex plans, extensibility, and parallel query execution into a durable foundation for engine design.
- [Volcano—An Extensible and Parallel Query Evaluation System (1994)](https://doi.org/10.1109/69.273032): Introduces the iterator (open-next-close) model where every operator implements the same pull-based interface, letting query plans compose arbitrarily and parallelize by inserting exchange operators — the execution model most DBMSs still use.
- [The Cascades Framework for Query Optimization (1995)](https://www.sigmod.org/publications/dblp/db/journals/debu/Graefe95a.html): Defines the extensible memo-based optimizer framework whose separation of logical transformations, physical implementations, enforcers, properties, and guided search shaped many production query optimizers.
- [Database Architecture Optimized for the New Bottleneck: Memory Access (1999)](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/11189/): A foundational hardware-conscious database paper that identifies memory latency as the new bottleneck and turns that diagnosis into vertically partitioned storage and cache-efficient radix join algorithms.
- [Eddies: Continuously Adaptive Query Processing (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1145/342009.335420): Replaces a fixed query plan with adaptive tuple routing, allowing execution to react continuously to changing selectivities and operator performance.
- [MonetDB/X100: Hyper-Pipelining Query Execution (2005)](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2005/papers/P19.pdf): Shows that processing data in small vectorized batches instead of tuple-at-a-time avoids the interpretation overhead of Volcano-style iterators and keeps data in CPU cache, delivering order-of-magnitude speedups.
- [Efficiently Compiling Efficient Query Plans for Modern Hardware (2011)](https://doi.org/10.14778/2002938.2002940): Compiles query plans directly to machine code via LLVM instead of interpreting an operator tree, organizing execution around data instead of operators — the design behind HyPer and later most high-performance analytical engines.
- [Morsel-Driven Parallelism: A NUMA-Aware Query Evaluation Framework for the Many-Core Age (2014)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2588555.2610507): Establishes morsel-driven execution as a practical way to obtain elastic, NUMA-aware parallelism and robust load balancing for analytical queries on many-core machines.
- [How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really? (2015)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol9/p204-leis.pdf): Uses the Join Order Benchmark to separate the effects of cardinality estimation, cost models, and plan enumeration, demonstrating that estimation errors are often the dominant cause of bad plans.
- [Everything You Always Wanted to Know About Compiled and Vectorized Queries But Were Afraid to Ask (2018)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol11/p2209-kersten.pdf): An apples-to-apples experimental comparison of vectorized execution and data-centric compilation that isolates their architectural tradeoffs across cache behavior, instruction count, SIMD, and multicore scaling.
- [DuckDB: An Embeddable Analytical Database (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3299869.3320212): Embedded columnar OLAP in a single process; the vectorized execution of X100/MonetDB taken to its practical extreme.
- [SQL Has Problems. We Can Fix Them: Pipe Syntax In SQL (2024)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p4051-shute.pdf): Makes a pragmatic case for composable pipe-structured data flow inside SQL, retaining backward compatibility while removing clause-order rigidity and simplifying multi-stage analytical queries and language extensions.
- [Optimizing LLM Queries in Relational Data Analytics Workloads (2025)](https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2025): A direct bridge between traditional query optimization and analytical workloads that incorporate LLM calls.

### Replicated Data Types

- [Data Consistency for P2P Collaborative Editing (2006)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1180875.1180916): Introduces WOOT, a peer-to-peer text editing algorithm that converges without operational transformation by giving every character a unique identifier and never truly deleting it.
- [Eventually Consistent (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1435417.1435432): A practitioner's tour of the consistency spectrum between strong and eventual, and of the client-side guarantees that make weak consistency usable at Amazon scale.
- [Logoot: A Scalable Optimistic Replication Algorithm for Collaborative Editing on P2P Networks (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDCS.2009.75): Replaces WOOT's tombstones with dense, ordered position identifiers so that collaborative editing scales to large documents and many peers.
- [A Commutative Replicated Data Type for Cooperative Editing (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDCS.2009.20): Presents Treedoc, a shared text buffer whose concurrent inserts and deletes commute by design, an early example of what would be named a CRDT.
- [A Comprehensive Study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types (2011)](https://inria.hal.science/inria-00555588): The catalog of CRDT designs: counters, registers, sets (including the observed-remove set), maps, graphs, and sequences, each specified in both state-based and operation-based form.
- [Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-24550-3_29): Names and formalizes CRDTs, defines strong eventual consistency, and shows that state-based and operation-based replicated types are equivalent ways to achieve it.
- [Replicated Abstract Data Types: Building Blocks for Collaborative Applications (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpdc.2010.12.006): Defines replicated abstract data types, including the replicated growable array (RGA), the sequence design behind many later collaborative editors.
- [An Optimized Conflict-Free Replicated Set (2012)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.3368): Removes tombstones from the observed-remove set by summarizing removed elements with a version vector, the design most production add-wins sets use.
- [Making Operation-Based CRDTs Operation-Based (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-43352-2_11): Moves the causality bookkeeping of operation-based CRDTs into a reusable messaging layer, so the data types themselves ship only the operations.
- [Replicated Data Types: Specification, Verification, Optimality (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2535838.2535848): Gives replicated data types a formal specification framework, proves implementations correct against it, and proves lower bounds on the metadata they must keep.
- [Efficient State-Based CRDTs by Delta-Mutation (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-26850-7_5): Introduces delta-mutators, which let state-based CRDTs ship small deltas instead of their full state while keeping state-based convergence guarantees.
- [Specification and Complexity of Collaborative Text Editing (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2933057.2933090): Specifies what a replicated list for text editing must guarantee, proves RGA meets it, and shows a metadata lower bound for any implementation.
- [A Conflict-Free Replicated JSON Datatype (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TPDS.2017.2697382): Combines maps, lists, and registers into a CRDT for arbitrarily nested JSON documents, with formal semantics for concurrent edits; this is the basis of Automerge.
- [Pure Operation-Based Replicated Data Types (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.04469): Defines operation-based CRDTs whose state is just a partially ordered log of operations, compacted once causal stability shows no concurrent operation can still arrive.
- [Verifying Strong Eventual Consistency in Distributed Systems (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3133933): Mechanically verifies in Isabelle/HOL that RGA, a counter, and an OR-set converge, and makes the network assumptions behind that guarantee explicit.
- [Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-63962-8_185-1): A short, authoritative introduction to CRDTs: the problem, the state-based, operation-based, and delta designs, and where they are used.
- [Delta State Replicated Data Types (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpdc.2017.08.003): The full treatment of delta-state CRDTs, covering anti-entropy algorithms for shipping deltas, causal delta merging, and a portfolio of delta-enabled data types.
- [Efficient Synchronization of State-Based CRDTs (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDE.2019.00022): Uses join decompositions to find and send only the part of a CRDT state a peer is missing, fixing redundant transmission in classic delta-based synchronization.
- [Local-First Software: You Own Your Data, in Spite of the Cloud (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3359591.3359737): Sets out seven ideals for apps that keep data on users' devices yet still collaborate, and argues that CRDTs are the technology that makes this practical.

### Self Driving Databases

- [Automatic Database Management System Tuning Through Large-scale Machine Learning (2017)](https://db.cs.cmu.edu/papers/2017/p1009-van-aken.pdf): Introduces OtterTune, which automatically tunes DBMS configuration parameters by reusing tuning data from other sessions — a practical proof of concept for the self-driving vision from CIDR 2017.
- [Self-Driving Database Management Systems (2017)](https://db.cs.cmu.edu/papers/2017/p42-pavlo-cidr17.pdf): Introduces Peloton, the 'first self-driving DBMS,' using deep learning to forecast workloads and reconfigure the system autonomously — a direct architectural successor to H-Store within CMU's database group.
- [Make Your Database System Dream of Electric Sheep: Towards Self-Driving Operation (2021)](https://doi.org/10.14778/3476311.3476411): Advances the self-driving DBMS vision into the NoisePage architecture, integrating forecasting, behavior modeling, and planning inside the database.

### Storage Engines

- [The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree) (1996)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s002360050048): Introduces the LSM-tree, batching random writes into sequential log merges to trade read amplification for write throughput — the storage structure underneath nearly every modern NoSQL and time-series database.
- [The Five-Minute Rule Ten Years Later, and Other Computer Storage Rules of Thumb (1997)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/the-five-minute-rule-ten-years-later/): Translates hardware price and performance ratios into practical rules for deciding when data belongs in memory, how large index pages should be, and how storage-system tradeoffs evolve with technology.
- [Modern B-Tree Techniques (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1561/1900000028): A comprehensive reference that goes far beyond textbook B-trees to cover transactional techniques, recovery, bulk and online utilities, advanced key structures, hardware effects, and robust query-processing uses.
- [bLSM: A General Purpose Log Structured Merge Tree (2012)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2213836.2213862): Turns the original LSM design into a practical general-purpose store with Bloom filters and a compaction scheduler designed to bound merge latency and avoid the severe write stalls common in early implementations.
- [The Adaptive Radix Tree: ARTful Indexing for Main-Memory Databases (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDE.2013.6544812): Introduces a radix tree whose node representation adapts to local fanout, combining cache-efficient point lookups with ordered scans and compact memory use.
- [The Bw-Tree: A B-tree for New Hardware Platforms (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDE.2013.6544834): Replaces in-place page updates and latches with indirection and delta records, adapting B-tree indexing to multicore processors and flash storage.
- [In-Memory Performance for Big Data (2014)](https://research.google/pubs/in-memory-performance-for-big-data/): Shows how pointer swizzling can nearly eliminate buffer-pool overhead for resident data while retaining transparent secondary-storage support and graceful degradation when a working set outgrows memory.
- [Design Tradeoffs of Data Access Methods (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2882903.2912569): A tutorial that walks through how tree, hash, LSM, bitmap, and adaptive access methods trade read cost against update cost and space, and how hardware and workload shifts move the balance.
- [Designing Access Methods: The RUM Conjecture (2016)](https://doi.org/10.5441/002/edbt.2016.42): Conjectures that an access method cannot minimize read, update, and memory overhead at once, since bounding any two sets a floor on the third, and maps B-trees, LSM-trees, hashing, and bitmaps onto that tradeoff space.
- [I/O Characteristics of MongoDB and Trim-Based Optimization in Flash SSDs (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3007818.3007844): Examines WiredTiger's collection, index, journal, and checkpoint I/O patterns, then shows how coordinating its space reclamation with SSD TRIM affects performance.
- [WiscKey: Separating Keys from Values in SSD-Conscious Storage (2016)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast16/technical-sessions/presentation/lu): Separates values into an append-only log while retaining keys in the LSM tree, sharply reducing compaction write amplification and exploiting SSD random-read parallelism at the cost of new garbage-collection and scan tradeoffs.
- [Monkey: Optimal Navigable Key-Value Store (2017)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3035918.3064054): Replaces uniform Bloom-filter allocation with a cost-derived distribution across levels, revealing how a small change in memory placement can exponentially reduce lookup cost and making LSM tuning an explicit optimization problem.
- [PebblesDB: Building Key-Value Stores Using Fragmented Log-Structured Merge Trees (2017)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3132747.3132765): Introduces fragmented LSM trees and guards to reduce compaction work and write amplification, illustrating the throughput-versus-read-cost tradeoff of relaxing globally sorted levels.
- [Better Space-Time Trade-Offs for LSM-Tree Based Key-Value Stores via Adaptive Removal of Superfluous Merging (2018)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3183713.3196927): Generalizes leveling and tiering into a continuum of merge policies and introduces lazy leveling, showing how to navigate update, lookup, and space amplification tradeoffs instead of committing to one fixed compaction strategy.
- [HOT: A Height Optimized Trie Index for Main-Memory Database Systems (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3183713.3196896): Varies the number of discriminating bits per trie node to retain high fanout, low height, and compact SIMD-friendly search for sparse string keys.
- [LeanStore: In-Memory Data Management beyond Main Memory (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDE.2018.00026): Combines in-memory data-structure speed with transparent eviction to SSD, showing how a lean buffer manager can span memory and storage efficiently.
- [SuRF: Practical Range Query Filtering with Fast Succinct Tries (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3183713.3196931): Extends approximate filtering beyond point membership by encoding an ordered key set as a compact trie that can reject empty range queries before storage access.
- [X-Engine: An Optimized Storage Engine for Large-scale E-commerce Transaction Processing (2019)](https://users.cs.utah.edu/~lifeifei/papers/sigmod-xengine.pdf): An LSM-tree storage engine with FPGA-accelerated compaction, built to survive extreme write bursts like Alibaba's Double 11 shopping festival — one of the first storage-engine kernel papers from a mainland Chinese company at a top-tier database venue.
- [LSM-based Storage Techniques: A Survey (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00778-019-00555-y): Organizes decades of LSM research into a practical taxonomy covering merge policies, Bloom filters, caching, secondary indexes, hardware awareness, and representative systems, making it the best map of the design space after the original paper.
- [Order-Preserving Key Compression for In-Memory Search Trees (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3318464.3380583): Compresses variable-length keys without changing their sort order, allowing existing tries and B-trees to use less memory while continuing to compare encoded keys directly.
- [Memory-Efficient Search Trees for Database Management Systems (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3448016.3461470): Synthesizes succinct static trees, update-friendly hybrid indexing, and order-preserving compression into a unified account of reducing DBMS index memory.
- [Evolution of Development Priorities in Key-Value Stores Serving Large-Scale Applications: The RocksDB Experience (2021)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast21/presentation/dong): A production retrospective explaining how RocksDB's priorities shifted from write amplification to space and CPU efficiency, and why compatibility, shared resource control, replication support, backups, and early corruption detection became first-class concerns.
- [Trie Memtables in Cassandra (2022)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.14778/3554821.3554828): Replaces Cassandra's skip-list partition map with sharded byte-comparable tries, shrinking heap pressure while accelerating reads and writes.
- [DILI: A Distribution-Driven Learned Index (2023)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol16/p2212-li.pdf): Builds an update-capable learned tree whose fanout and leaf models follow local key distributions, balancing model accuracy against traversal depth.
- [Making In-Memory Learned Indexes Efficient on Disk (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3654954): Derives six storage-aware transformations that turn memory-first learned indexes into disk layouts that improve both throughput and space over B+ trees.
- [Memento Filter: A Fast, Dynamic, and Robust Range Filter (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3698820): Makes range filtering dynamic and workload-robust, extending the idea beyond static LSM components to changing B-tree indexes such as WiredTiger.
- [Accelerating String-key Learned Index Structures via Memoization-based Incremental Training (2024)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p1802-park.pdf): Reuses prior model-training work for updated string keys and offloads retraining to an FPGA, attacking the cost that makes mutable string learned indexes impractical.
- [Towards Systematic Index Dynamization (2024)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p2867-rumbaugh.pdf): Turns specialized static indexes into update-capable structures through a configurable dynamization framework, narrowing the gap from research prototype to deployable index.
- [DobLIX: A Dual-Objective Learned Index for Log-Structured Merge Trees (2025)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p3965-heidari.pdf): Co-optimizes learned-model accuracy and physical block access inside RocksDB, adapting its LSM index and data layout as workloads change.
- [FB+-tree: A Memory-Optimized B+-tree with Latch-Free Update (2025)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p1579-li.pdf): Blends trie-like byte-wise branching with a balanced B+ tree and latch-free updates to improve cache behavior and multicore scalability under contention.

### Streaming Dataflow

- [Discretized Streams: Fault-Tolerant Streaming Computation at Scale (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2517349.2522737): Reframes stream processing as deterministic sequences of small batch computations, enabling recovery through lineage instead of continuous operator replication.
- [MillWheel: Fault-Tolerant Stream Processing at Internet Scale (2013)](https://doi.org/10.14778/2536222.2536229): Fault-tolerant streaming with watermarks and persistent state; a direct precursor to the Dataflow model.
- [Naiad: A Timely Dataflow System (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2517349.2522738): A timely dataflow model that adds a logical timestamp to every dataflow edge, letting one engine express batch, streaming, and iterative/graph computations with low-latency incremental updates.
- [The Dataflow Model: A Practical Approach to Balancing Correctness, Latency, and Cost in Massive-Scale, Unbounded, Out-of-Order Data Processing (2015)](https://doi.org/10.14778/2824032.2824076): Unified batch and streaming into a single model of windows and event time; the conceptual basis for Beam and Flink.
- [Foundations of Differential Dataflow (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-46678-0_5): Gives a formal account of differential dataflow's ability to maintain iterative computations efficiently as input collections change.
- [Apache Flink: Stream and Batch Processing in a Single Engine (2015)](https://asterios.katsifodimos.com/assets/publications/flink-deb.pdf): An engine that treats batch as a special case of streaming; consistent snapshots via distributed checkpointing.
- [MacroBase: Prioritizing Attention in Fast Data (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3035918.3035928): Builds a streaming analytics engine that searches for and explains anomalies directly, rather than requiring an analyst to already know which query would have found them.
- [Noria: Dynamic, Partially-Stateful Data-Flow for High-Performance Web Applications (2018)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi18/presentation/gjengset): Applies incremental-dataflow ideas (in the vein of CIEL/Naiad) as a storage backend for read-heavy web applications, introducing 'partially stateful' dataflow that evicts and reconstructs materialized state on demand.

### Streaming Log

- [Kafka: A Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing (2011)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Kafka.pdf): Treats the commit log itself as the product — a distributed, partitioned, append-only log that consumers read at their own pace, replacing point-to-point messaging with a durable, replayable stream.
- [Open-Sourcing Pulsar: Pub-Sub Messaging at Scale (2017)](https://yahooeng.tumblr.com/post/150078336821/open-sourcing-pulsar-pub-sub-messaging-at-scale): Separates stateless message serving from durable BookKeeper storage, enabling multi-tenant messaging and independent scaling of brokers and persistence.
- [Samza: Stateful Scalable Stream Processing at LinkedIn (2017)](https://doi.org/10.14778/3137765.3137770): A stream processor built directly on Kafka for both messaging and durable local state, using changelog topics to make stateful operators recoverable without a separate state-management system.

### Systems Design Principles

- [Hints for Computer System Design (1983)](https://doi.org/10.1145/773379.806614): Distills durable rules for interfaces, correctness, recovery, and performance that remain useful when reasoning about complex distributed systems.
- [End-to-End Arguments in System Design (1984)](https://doi.org/10.1145/357401.357402): Argues that correctness-critical functions like reliable delivery should live at the endpoints of a system, not be pushed into lower layers that can't fully guarantee them — a principle that shaped the Internet's own design.
- [Life Beyond Distributed Transactions: An Apostate's Opinion (2007)](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2007/papers/cidr07p15.pdf): A provocative essay on designing systems that avoid distributed transactions. Sparks discussion even in a small group.
- [The Tail at Scale (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2408776.2408794): Why tail latency dominates in large services and how 'tail tolerance' techniques attack it. Short and influential.

### Transactions Recovery

- [Granularity of Locks and Degrees of Consistency in a Shared Data Base (1976)](https://doi.org/10.1145/1282480.1282513): Defines lock granularity and degrees of consistency — vocabulary still used for isolation levels today.
- [The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations (1981)](https://www.vldb.org/conf/1981/P144.PDF): Jim Gray's early statement of what a transaction actually guarantees (atomicity, durability, and what would later be codified as ACID) and where the abstraction breaks down for long-running or nested work.
- [ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging (1992)](https://doi.org/10.1145/128765.128770): Introduces write-ahead logging with LSNs, physiological logging, and fuzzy checkpointing — the recovery algorithm underlying most commercial databases' crash recovery to this day.
- [Instant Recovery with Write-Ahead Logging (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13222-015-0204-3): Makes database pages available on demand during restart, reducing the outage imposed by traditional log recovery without abandoning write-ahead logging.

### Vector Databases

- [DiskANN: Fast Accurate Billion-Point Nearest Neighbor Search on a Single Node (2019)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/hash/09853c7fb1d3f8ee67a61b6bf4a7f8e6-Abstract.html): Makes billion-scale graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor search practical on one SSD-backed machine through a storage-aware index layout.
- [Milvus: A Purpose-Built Vector Data Management System (2021)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3448016.3457550): A data management system purpose-built for large-scale approximate nearest-neighbor search over vectors — the data-infrastructure piece underneath embeddings, semantic search, and RAG in the modern AI stack.
- [VBASE: Unifying Online Vector Similarity Search and Relational Queries via Relaxed Monotonicity (2023)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi23/presentation/zhang-qianxi): Identifies relaxed monotonicity as the key to integrating approximate vector indexes with complex relational query execution efficiently.
- [Survey of Vector Database Management Systems (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00778-024-00864-x): Organizes vector database designs across indexing, storage, query processing, optimization, and distributed execution, providing a map for reading individual systems papers.

## Curated relations

How papers relate, in the curator's words. `contradicts` and `refines` mark disagreements worth reading side by side.

- Amazon DynamoDB: A Scalable, Predictably Performant, and Fully Managed NoSQL Database Service (2022) supersedes Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (2007)
- Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database (2012) contradicts Life Beyond Distributed Transactions: An Apostate's Opinion (2007)
- In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft) (2014) simplifies Viewstamped Replication: A New Primary Copy Method to Support Highly-Available Distributed Systems (1988)

## Optional

- [Schema reference](https://github.com/eribeiro/reading-tracks/blob/main/SCHEMA.md): field-level data format
